findings.old_behavior: parseInteger() passed the input string directly to strtoul(), which silently wraps negative signed values to large unsigned values. For example, --max-ampl -1 set the amplification limit to ULONG_MAX, effectively disabling the protection. --maxmem -1 similarly assigned an enormous memory limit.
findings.new_behavior: parseInteger() now checks for a leading '\-' character before calling strtoul(). If a negative value is detected, it prints an error message ("<context>: value not allowed: <value>") to errStream and returns -1, rejecting the input.
findings.compatibility_reason: CLI options --maxmem, --pretty, and --max-ampl use parseInteger() to parse their arguments. Previously, negative values were silently accepted via strtoul() wrapping. Now they are rejected with an error. Any script, wrapper, or user relying on passing negative values to these options (even accidentally) will experience a behavior change — the command will now fail with an error message instead of silently proceeding with a wrapped value.
findings.why_not_internal_only: parseInteger() is a static function but is called by CLI option handlers for --maxmem (line 2614), --pretty (line 2803), and --max-ampl (line 2911), making it part of the public CLI surface. The CLI surface is defined as public in the libxml2 effective profile (cli_options surface).
findings.uncertainty: Low uncertainty. The behavior change is clearly visible in the diff. The only uncertainty is whether any caller relied on the wrapping behavior, which is unlikely as the wrapping was a bug (per the commit message fixing a security issue).
findings.recommended_review: Review any scripts or test suites that pass negative values to --maxmem, --pretty, or --max-ampl. These will now fail with an error.
findings.test_recommendation: Verify that xmllint --maxmem -1, xmllint --pretty -1, and xmllint --max-ampl -1 all produce error messages and exit with non-zero status. Verify that positive values and zero continue to work as before. Check boundary values (e.g., --maxmem 0, --maxmem 1, --maxmem <actual limit>).
